new.title: Walk into Mainz Cathedral's thousand-year story
new.desc: Archbishop Willigis ordered the cathedral in 975, and after a fire on the day of its first inauguration it was finished by 1036. Inside lie archbishop-electors and Johannes Gutenberg, and the cloister houses the cathedral museum.
new.tip: Go in the morning before the market crowds. Look up at the St. Martin statue on the western roof, then step into the cloister.

new.title: Stand in Chagall's blue light at St. Stephan
new.desc: Founded by Willigis in 990, this is the oldest Gothic hall church on the Upper Rhine. Marc Chagall made nine blue windows with Old Testament figures here between 1978 and 1985, meant as a sign of Jewish-German reconciliation.
new.tip: Sit down in the choir and let the blue settle. Weddings can close the church on some Saturday afternoons, so a weekday visit is safest.

new.title: Look up at the ceiling and crypt of St. Ignaz
new.desc: This classicist church was built between 1763 and 1775 and has a ceiling painted with scenes from the life of St. Ignatius. Below the choir is a crypt where 198 of the original 261 oven-shaped graves survive.
new.tip: Check opening times first, since small churches close at odd hours. The ceiling is best seen from the middle of the nave.

new.title: Admire the great dome of the Christuskirche
new.desc: Built from 1896 to 1903 in Italian High Renaissance style, this Protestant church has a dome about 80 m high that was meant to rival the cathedral. It was destroyed in the air raid of 1 February 1945 and rebuilt in the early 1950s.
new.tip: Walk up Kaiserstraße for the best view of the dome. The Bachchor Mainz sings and plays concerts here.

new.title: Find the warning on the Renaissance Marktbrunnen
new.desc: Cardinal Albrecht von Brandenburg donated this red sandstone fountain in 1526, partly to mark the end of the Peasants' War. A carving of a drunken peasant carries the warning to remember the end.
new.tip: Look at the pillar reliefs, with skulls and hourglasses, from the cathedral side of the market square.

new.title: Count the jesters on the Fastnachtsbrunnen
new.desc: Unveiled on 14 January 1967, this bronze tower almost nine metres tall carries more than 200 figures from carnival life, from a fool riding a donkey backwards to the motto Weck, Worscht un Woi. It is said to look like the cathedral turned upside down.
new.tip: Walk all the way round it, then compare it with the Schiller monument that frames the square.

new.title: Meet the two stone lions of the Eisenturm
new.desc: The Iron Tower is one of only three surviving towers of the medieval city wall and dates to around 1200. A late Romanesque lion with a ram and another with a dragon flank the portal, and the tower now hosts an art association.
new.tip: Pass by on the way along Rheinstraße and compare it with the Holzturm, a ten-minute walk away.

new.title: Peer at the prison tower of Schinderhannes
new.desc: The Holzturm gained its Gothic look in the early 15th century. The outlaw Schinderhannes was held here for more than 15 months before his execution in 1803. The old gateway now lies about three metres below street level.
new.tip: The tower is not open to the public, so admire it from outside and notice how the street has risen.

new.title: Explore the 17th century Zitadelle
new.desc: This fortress was converted into a regular quadrangular citadel around 1655 and was held by the French army until 1955. You can see the main gate, the 1696 Kommandantenbau, bastions and old air raid shelters in the casemates.
new.tip: Walk the ramparts on a dry day. The Open Ohr youth festival has been held here since 1975.

new.title: Find the Roman Drususstein inside the Zitadelle
new.desc: This is the stump of a Roman cenotaph that legionaries raised for Nero Claudius Drusus, who died in 9 BC. It was left untouched when the citadel was built around it.
new.tip: Look for it on the Bastion Drusus. The city history museum stands close by.

new.title: Stand beside the Roman theatre of Mogontiacum
new.desc: With a diameter of about 116 m and room for roughly 10,000 spectators, this was the largest Roman stage theatre north of the Alps. Rediscovered in the 1880s and 1914, it has been excavated since 1999.
new.tip: It sits next to Mainz Römisches Theater station, so it is a quick stop on any train.
new.q: Römisches Theater, Bahnhof Mainz Römisches Theater, Mainz

new.title: Walk over a Roman temple of Isis in a shopping mall
new.desc: A glass walkway runs above the reassembled Roman sanctuary of Isis and Mater Magna in the basement of the Römerpassage. It was found in 1999, and 34 lead curse tablets were dug from its offering pits.
new.tip: Entry is free, and the audio guide is told by a fictional Roman citizen. A good rainy day stop.
new.q: Heiligtum der Isis und Mater Magna, Römerpassage 1, Mainz

new.title: See five Roman warships at the ancient seafaring museum
new.desc: Remains of five late Roman warships were found in 1981 and 1982 and are shown with full size replicas, including a navis lusoria. The museum sits in a former locomotive repair hall near the Roman theatre.
new.tip: The museum has been closed for renovation, so check its website for the reopening date before you go.
new.q: Museum für Antike Schifffahrt, Neutorstraße 2b, Mainz

new.title: Browse Roman stones at the Landesmuseum Mainz
new.desc: In the former electoral stables, nicknamed the Golden Ross barracks, you find more than 2,000 Roman stone monuments, an Orpheus mosaic and Jugendstil glass. The Judaica collection includes a gravestone dated 1049.
new.tip: Allow two hours. The Orpheus mosaic and the Roman stone hall are the highlights.

new.title: Watch a Gutenberg press at the Gutenberg Museum
new.desc: The museum was founded in 1900 and holds a Gutenberg Bible and a replica of his press in a reconstructed workshop. While the main building is being replaced, a part of the collection is shown as Gutenberg-Museum MOVED next to the natural history museum.
new.tip: Check current hours and book the Druckladen print workshop in advance. A great rainy day stop.

new.title: Try on carnival history at the Fastnachtsmuseum
new.desc: In a renovated Proviant-Magazin, about 350 square metres of exhibits tell the history of Mainz carnival since 1837, with fool's caps, scepters, guard uniforms and videos. The affiliated archive holds more than 27,000 items.
new.tip: Come in the weeks before 11 November for the full mood. Entry is cheap.

new.title: See contemporary art in the old Kunsthalle power house
new.desc: Opened in 2008, the Kunsthalle fills a boiler and machine house planned by Eduard Kreyßig in 1887. Berlin architects added a 21 m tower tilted by seven degrees, and the old locomotive shed is now a cafe.
new.tip: Pair it with a walk along the Zollhafen harbour. Exhibitions change, so check what is on.

new.title: Hike to the Römersteine aqueduct pillars
new.desc: The Römersteine are the remains of a Roman aqueduct that supplied the legionary camp. Up to 25 m high, they are called the highest of their kind north of the Alps, and about 69 pillars survive.
new.tip: Take tram 52 to the Römersteine stop.

new.title: Visit Judensand, one of Europe's oldest Jewish cemeteries
new.desc: The Judensand is the oldest known burial ground of Mainz's Jewish community and part of the UNESCO SchUM sites since 2021. Its oldest surviving gravestone dates to 1049 and is kept in the Landesmuseum.
new.tip: Dress and behave respectfully. The memorial stones are not aligned east because they were moved.

new.title: Wander the University Botanical Garden
new.desc: About 10 hectares and roughly 8,500 plant species, with greenhouses from the 1940s and 1950s, a frog pond, an arboretum and a replica of the Mainzer Sand dune habitat.
new.tip: The outdoor garden is free. Guided tours are offered, so check the website for dates.

new.title: Stroll through the Stadtpark above the Rhine
new.desc: The Stadtpark was laid out in English landscape style between 1819 and 1825 by Peter Wolf. It has a rose garden from 1925, a small zoo and a palm house.
new.tip: It is a calm green stretch near the Rhine. Late summer brings the Weinmarkt here.

new.title: Find the Roman city gate at Am Römertor
new.desc: Remains of a late antique Roman city gate stand on the Kästrich hill, a trace of the walls of Mogontiacum.
new.tip: Pair it with a walk along the Kästrich and the nearby Gautor.

new.title: Wander the half-timbered lanes of the Kirschgarten
new.desc: This old town square dates back to 1329 and is lined with half-timbered houses from the 15th to 18th centuries. Haus Zum Aschaffenburg from around 1500 is the oldest partly preserved half-timbered house in Mainz.
new.tip: Come in the early evening when the lanes are quiet. Look for the Madonna fountain from 1932.

new.title: Stroll along Augustinerstraße and its wine taverns
new.desc: The main street of Mainz's southern old town was the main shopping street until the 17th century. Houses from around 1687 and the Baroque Augustinerkirche line a lane that is now full of cafes, shops and wine houses.
new.tip: Walk it from the south end and duck into side lanes. Evenings are lively.

new.title: Visit the Reduit fortress across the bridge in Kastel
new.desc: This fortification from 1832 protected the old pontoon bridge. Today the Museum Castellum inside is free on Sundays.
new.tip: Walk across the Theodor-Heuss-Brücke. Open hours are limited, so check before you go.

new.title: Lounge on the Strand at Bastion von Schönborn
new.desc: On the Kastel Rhine bank, the bastion has a free beach with loungers and a restaurant. You may not eat food brought from outside.
new.tip: Best on a warm evening for sunset views over the Mainz skyline.

new.title: Walk the Brückentour over the Rhine
new.desc: This route of about 7 km crosses the Theodor-Heuss-Brücke, passes the Reduit and the Maaraue, and returns by the railway bridge. The bridge was rebuilt in the early 1950s.
new.tip: Start at the Rathaus side of the Rhine promenade. Bring water in summer.

new.title: Descend into the Kupferberg sparkling wine cellars
new.desc: Founded in 1850, Kupferberg has cellars said to be the deepest sparkling wine cellars in the world, with seven levels reaching down about 50 m. A museum shows the largest known collection of sparkling wine glasses.
new.tip: Guided tours of the museum and cellars are run via the on-site brewery. Book ahead and bring a jacket.

new.title: Catch a show at the Staatstheater Mainz
new.desc: This theatre was built from 1829 to 1833 and rebuilt after the war. A glass rotunda was added in 1998 and the Deck 3 studio on top opened in 2012.
new.tip: Check the season and buy tickets online. The foyer is worth a look even before a show.

new.title: Greet the Gutenberg monument on Gutenbergplatz
new.desc: The monument stands on the square in front of the Staatstheater and honours the inventor of movable type.
new.tip: Pair it with the printing museum and the cathedral, both a short walk away.

new.title: Browse the cathedral market on Markt
new.desc: On Tuesday, Friday and Saturday from 7 to 14 the market fills the squares around the cathedral. Fish rolls and local plums are among the stalls.
new.tip: Plums are often cheaper after 13:00. Saturday is the busiest.

new.title: Join the Saturday Marktfrühstück with local winegrowers
new.desc: The Mainzer Winzer, 23 wine estates from the city, serve wine with Weck, Worscht un Woi on Saturday mornings on old town squares. The sites include Schillerplatz.
new.tip: Check which winemakers are at which square that day. The season runs from spring to autumn.

new.title: Raise a mug at the Eisgrub brewery
new.desc: The Eisgrub-Bräu is a brewery tavern in an old ice cellar, brewing since 1872. It serves pale and dark beer by the glass or up to 3 litres, with hearty regional food.
new.tip: Order a Handkäs mit Musik. Open every day from late morning.

new.title: Dine in the 800 year old Heiliggeist hospital hall
new.desc: The Heilig-Geist-Spital was handed over in 1236 and has a late Romanesque shell with a Gothic hall inside. It is a listed building and has had a restaurant on the ground floor since 1863.
new.tip: Come at lunch for the high vaulted hall. Book for evenings.

new.title: Taste Rheinhessen wines at Gebert's Weinstuben
new.desc: This wine tavern on Frauenlobstraße is known for a German wine list and traditional dishes such as Handkäs soup and wild boar.
new.tip: Reserve a table and check the closing days before you go.

new.title: Taste a Rheinhessen Riesling at Weinstube Hottum
new.desc: A cosy old town wine tavern said to date from 1791 that serves only Rheingau and Rheinhessen wines. It sits just off Augustinerstraße.
new.tip: Go in the evening and ask for the Handkäs mit Musik.

new.title: Order Handkäs at the old Weinhaus Wilhelmi
new.desc: Founded in 1894, this wood-panelled wine house on Spitalgasse has been called one of the oldest in Mainz, and its Handkäs has been praised as perhaps the best in the city.
new.tip: Spundekäs is served outside in summer.

new.title: Share a Spundekäs at Weinhaus zum Spiegel
new.desc: This old town Weinhaus on Leichhofstraße serves Handkäs with or without music and a homemade Spundekäs.
new.tip: Come in the evening and check the closing days.

new.title: Watch Rhine barges at the Mole Biergarten
new.desc: This beer garden sits on the Winterhafen at the Rhine. You drink beer and snack while watching shipping go by.
new.tip: Go on a summer evening.
new.q: Mole Biergarten am Winterhafen, Victor-Hugo-Ufer, Mainz

new.title: Queue for unusual flavours at N'Eis
new.desc: A popular Neustadt ice cream parlour known for unusual flavours. Expect queues in summer.
new.tip: Visit after a stroll through the Neustadt.

new.title: Eat schnitzel at the Am Holztor wine tavern
new.desc: A traditional tavern on Holzstraße, praised for schnitzel and chicken, with an English menu.
new.tip: Sit down after seeing the Holzturm, just up the street.

new.title: Sit in the classic Augustinerkeller
new.desc: A classic Gaststätte with old pictures of Mainz on the walls, on Augustinerstraße. The building incorporates vaulted cellars of an older court.
new.tip: Order a regional dish and a glass of Rheinhessen wine.

new.title: Try the nine sauces at Best Worscht in Town
new.desc: A currywurst spot on Augustinerstraße with homemade bread and nine sauces whose heat you can adjust.
new.tip: Start mild. The heat can be intense.
new.q: Best Worscht in Town, Augustinerstraße 11, Mainz

new.title: Drink a craft beer at the Eulchen brewery in the Kupferberg
new.desc: Eulchen brewing is based in the old Kupferberg administration building from 1856, and a brewery tap serves its beers.
new.tip: Combine it with a Kupferberg cellar tour.

new.title: Relax in the Zum Goldstein beer garden
new.desc: A pleasant beer garden in a quiet side street of the old town.
new.tip: Visit on a warm evening.

new.title: Taste your way through the Mainzer Weinmarkt
new.desc: Held in the Stadtpark on the last weekend of August and the first weekend of September, this wine fair lets you sample local wines.
new.tip: Bring cash and plan a ride home.

new.title: Walk the grounds of Charlemagne's Ingelheim palace
new.desc: Charlemagne first stayed at Ingelheim in 774 and wintered here in 787 to 788. An imperial palace complex with a 40 m long Aula regia stood here, and the Romanesque palace church is still in use.
new.tip: The grounds are freely accessible, and a museum at the palace shows finds.

new.title: Climb the Bismarckturm above Ingelheim
new.desc: Built between 1907 and 1912 by Wilhelm Kreis, this 31 m tower has 124 steps and an observation platform at about 22 m.
new.tip: Climb on a clear day.

new.title: Marvel at the Katharinenkirche rose window in Oppenheim
new.desc: The Katharinenkirche is called one of the most important Gothic churches on the Rhine. Its rose window from 1332 is largely original, and nearby St. Michael's Chapel has an ossuary holding the bones of about 20,000 people.
new.tip: Visit the chapel ossuary next door. Allow an hour for the old town.

new.title: Climb to Burg Landskron above Oppenheim
new.desc: This 13th century castle was blown up by French troops in 1689. You can see a 40 m deep well, the palace walls and a viewing platform.
new.tip: On clear days, the view reaches the Odenwald and Worms Cathedral.

new.title: Descend into the Oppenheim Kellerlabyrinth
new.desc: About 40 km of cellars, passages and stairs lie under the town on up to five levels, carved from loess. Tours run in groups of around 20.
new.tip: The cellar is about 17 degrees all year, so bring a jacket. Join a guided tour.

new.title: Hike the Roter Hang above the Rhine
new.desc: The Roter Hang is a 5 km strip of steep red slopes between Nackenheim and Nierstein, with sites like Brudersberg and Pettenthal. Riesling is the main grape.
new.tip: A hiking trail links Nackenheim and Nierstein. Wear sturdy shoes.

new.title: Spot the Mäuseturm on its Rhine island
new.desc: This small tower on an island near Bingen was a customs tower from 1298 and was rebuilt in 1855 as a Prussian signal tower. The legend tells of Archbishop Hatto and a swarm of mice.
new.tip: See it from the Park am Mäuseturm riverside.

new.title: Climb the Rochusberg to its neo-Gothic chapel
new.desc: The Rochuskapelle was built from 1893 to 1895 after a fire in 1889. Goethe described the Rochusfest in 1814, and the chapel belongs to the Upper Middle Rhine UNESCO site.
new.tip: Come for the hilltop setting above Bingen. The Rochusfest is held on two weekends in August.

new.title: Look over Bingen from Burg Klopp
new.desc: This castle, built from 1240 to 1277, now houses the city administration, with a keep above the town.
new.tip: Combine it with the Museum am Strom and the Rhine promenade.

new.title: Climb the Wartbergturm above Alzey
new.desc: This tower, 28 m tall with 115 steps, was built in 1988 and 1989. From the platform you see the Rheinhessen hills, the Donnersberg and the Taunus.
new.tip: On clear days the Frankfurt skyline shows.

new.title: Find the Trullo vineyard hut near Flonheim
new.desc: The Weißes Häuschen trullo near Flonheim is thought to have been built by Italian workers. A wine hike is held here in spring.
new.tip: Wear walking shoes and bring a picnic.

new.title: Walk through the steppe dunes of the Mainzer Sand
new.desc: A nature reserve of about 127 hectares of inland dunes with relic steppe plants such as the sand lotwurz. It lies between Gonsenheim and Mombach.
new.tip: Spring brings the best flowers. Stay on the paths.

new.title: Taste Riesling at Weingut Gunderloch in Nackenheim
new.desc: Founded in 1890 by a Mainz banker, this estate in Nackenheim farms about 14 hectares, including sites in Pettenthal and Hipping on the Roter Hang. Riesling is about 80 percent of plantings.
new.tip: A guided tasting of four estate wines is offered. Book in advance.

new.title: Sip Roter Hang Riesling at Weingut St. Antony
new.desc: This organic estate in Nierstein has about 60 hectares, mostly on the Roter Hang, and has been a VDP member since 1990.
new.tip: Ask about visits at the Vinothek. Plan for a taxi or the train.

new.title: Taste Ingelheim red wine at Weingut J. Neus
new.desc: Ingelheim is known for red wines, and this estate, founded in 1881, grows mostly Spätburgunder. An 1888 lexicon called the local Oberingelheimer Germany's second best red wine.
new.tip: Visit in autumn for the Rotweinfest season.
new.q: Weingut J. Neus, Bahnhofstraße 96, Ingelheim am Rhein
